introduction.content:
In the previous article, we established what a carbon credit is — a verified certificate representing one tonne of CO₂ removed or reduced. But a credit sitting in a registry account is not much use on its own.

For carbon credits to drive climate action at scale, they need to be tradeable. They need a price. They need buyers who want them and sellers who can produce them. In other words, they need a market.

Carbon markets are where that price gets discovered, where supply meets demand, and where the financial incentive to reduce emissions actually flows to the people doing the work. Understanding how these markets are structured — and the fundamental difference between the two main types — is essential for any business navigating climate compliance or voluntary decarbonisation.

This article explains how carbon markets work, who the participants are, what drives prices, and where India's rapidly developing market sits within the global picture.

sections.heading: What Is a Carbon Market?
sections.content:
A carbon market is a trading system in which carbon credits are bought and sold. Like any market, it has buyers, sellers, a unit of trade (the carbon credit), and a mechanism for discovering price.

But carbon markets differ from conventional commodity markets in one important way: the thing being traded — a verified emission reduction — has no physical form. You cannot see or touch a tonne of CO₂ that was prevented from entering the atmosphere. The entire system depends on the credibility of the measurement, verification, and registry infrastructure that sits behind each credit.

This dependence on credibility is why market structure, governance, and standards matter so much in carbon markets. A rice market can survive a bad batch of rice — the problem is visible and localised. A carbon market cannot as easily survive widespread questions about whether the credits being traded represent real reductions. Credibility is both the product and the foundation.

Carbon markets today are broadly divided into two types — compliance markets, created by governments, and voluntary markets, created by independent standards bodies. They operate in parallel, serve different buyers, trade different instruments, and have different price levels — but they are increasingly interconnected.

infoBox.title: Carbon Market
infoBox.content: A carbon market is a trading system where carbon credits — each representing one verified tonne of CO₂ equivalent reduced or removed — are bought and sold between participants. Price is determined by supply and demand, shaped by regulatory requirements, corporate commitments, and project economics.

sections.heading: The Two Types of Carbon Market
sections.content:
The most important thing to understand about carbon markets is that there are two fundamentally different types operating simultaneously — and confusing them leads to poor business decisions.

Compliance markets — also called regulated markets or cap-and-trade systems — are created by governments. Participation is mandatory for covered industries. Failing to hold enough credits results in regulatory penalties.

Voluntary carbon markets (VCM) are created by independent standards bodies. Participation is optional. Companies engage because of net-zero commitments, stakeholder expectations, or supply chain requirements — not legal obligation.

These two markets operate in parallel globally. A steel company in Germany participates in the EU Emissions Trading System (compliance). An airline buying offsets for its corporate travel programme participates in the voluntary market. The credits are different, the registries are different, the price levels are different, and the rules are different.

India, as of 2026, has both. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is India's compliance market, covering nine industrial sectors. The voluntary market exists in parallel, with Indian projects listed on international registries like Verra and Gold Standard, and Indian companies buying credits to meet voluntary net-zero commitments.

sections.heading: How Compliance Markets Work
sections.content:
A compliance market begins with a cap — a government-mandated limit on the total greenhouse gas emissions permitted across the covered sectors. This cap is set below current emission levels, creating scarcity that drives the market.

Within the cap, facilities receive or purchase allowances — the right to emit a specific quantity of CO₂. At the end of each compliance period, every covered facility must surrender allowances equal to its actual emissions. Emit more than your allowances cover, and you face a financial penalty. Emit less, and you have surplus allowances you can sell.

This is the mechanism that makes compliance markets powerful: by making excess emissions financially costly, they create a direct incentive to reduce. The penalty for non-compliance must exceed the cost of abatement for the market to work — regulators calibrate this carefully.

Over time, the cap is tightened — fewer allowances are issued each year. This creates increasing scarcity, driving prices higher, which in turn drives more aggressive emission reduction investment. The EU ETS, which started in 2005 with a carbon price under €5, had prices above €100 by 2023.

India's CCTS works slightly differently. Rather than a hard cap on total emissions, it uses Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI) targets — measuring emissions per unit of output. A steel plant is not told it can emit a maximum of X tonnes. It is told it must not emit more than Y tonnes per tonne of crude steel produced. This intensity-based approach accommodates economic growth while still driving efficiency improvements.

infoBox.title: Cap-and-Trade vs Intensity-Based — Why India Chose Differently
infoBox.content: Hard caps work well for mature economies with stable industrial output. India chose an intensity-based approach because it allows industrial production to grow while still reducing emission efficiency — a critical distinction for a developing economy with ambitious manufacturing expansion targets. As India's economy matures, the CCTS is expected to migrate toward absolute caps.

sections.heading: How Voluntary Markets Work
sections.content:
The voluntary carbon market operates without a government mandate. No regulator tells companies they must participate. Instead, companies choose to engage — typically because they have made a public net-zero or carbon neutrality commitment, face investor or supply chain pressure to demonstrate climate action, or wish to build ESG credentials ahead of anticipated regulation.

In the voluntary market, credits are generated by projects — the renewable energy installations, forest restoration programmes, methane capture facilities, and clean cookstove deployments described in the first article of this series. These projects register with an independent standard (Verra, Gold Standard, the American Carbon Registry) and go through the MRV process to generate tradeable credits.

Buyers access voluntary credits through several channels: directly from project developers, through brokers and trading desks, on digital exchanges, or through funds that aggregate credits across multiple projects.

The voluntary market has faced significant credibility challenges over the past five years. Investigative journalism in 2023 found that several large REDD+ forest protection programmes had overstated their emission reductions — issuing credits for forests that were never actually at risk. This prompted significant reform across major registries and the emergence of the ICVCM Core Carbon Principles (CCP) — a quality standard that credits must meet to be labelled as high-integrity.

The lesson for buyers is that not all voluntary credits are equal. Quality varies enormously, and price is an imperfect proxy. A credit that costs ₹400 may represent a real, permanent, additional emission reduction — or it may not. Due diligence on the project, methodology, verification body, and registry is essential.

mythVsFact.myth: Voluntary carbon markets are unregulated and therefore unreliable
mythVsFact.fact: Voluntary markets are not government-regulated, but they are not unregulated. Independent standards bodies (Verra, Gold Standard, ICVCM) set rigorous requirements for project design, verification, issuance, and retirement. The problem has been inconsistent enforcement — which is being addressed through the CCP framework and improved registry governance.

mythVsFact.myth: Compliance credits and voluntary credits are interchangeable
mythVsFact.fact: They are not. Compliance credits (like India's CCCs) are issued under government authority for use in meeting mandatory regulatory obligations. Voluntary credits (VCUs, GS VERs) are issued by independent registries for voluntary offsetting. They cannot generally be used interchangeably — a company cannot retire a Verra VCU to meet its CCTS obligation.

mythVsFact.myth: Buying cheap carbon credits is a cost-effective sustainability strategy
mythVsFact.fact: Cheap credits often reflect low quality — poor additionality, weak permanence, or inflated baselines. Using low-quality credits in sustainability claims exposes companies to reputational risk, litigation, and regulatory scrutiny. High-quality credits cost more but deliver the climate outcome they claim.

sections.heading: Who Participates in Carbon Markets?
sections.content:
Carbon markets involve a broader set of participants than most people expect. Understanding who each player is and what role they serve helps demystify how a project in Madhya Pradesh eventually ends up offsetting a multinational's Scope 3 emissions.

Project Developers design, fund, and operate the underlying emission reduction projects. They bear the upfront cost of project development, MRV, and verification, and receive credits in return. Developers range from large specialist firms with global project portfolios to individual landowners running small reforestation projects.

Verification and Validation Bodies (VVBs) are independent auditors accredited by registry standards. They validate project design before a project launches and verify monitoring reports before credits are issued. In India, organisations like Bureau Veritas, DNV, EY, and KPMG provide VVB services.

Registries maintain the definitive ledger of all carbon credits — issued, transferred, and retired. Verra, Gold Standard, and GRID-India (for CCTS) each operate their own registry. Each credit exists as a unique entry in a registry, with a serial number that tracks its entire history.

Brokers and Intermediaries facilitate transactions between project developers and buyers, particularly in the over-the-counter (OTC) market where large volumes are traded bilaterally. They provide price discovery and counterparty matching but also add cost and reduce transparency.

Exchanges provide a standardised, transparent venue for trading. The EU ETS trades on exchanges like ICE and EEX. India's CCTS trades on IEX and PXIL. Digital platforms like EtherTrack provide exchange infrastructure for both compliance and voluntary credits.

Corporate Buyers are the ultimate demand side — companies buying credits either to meet compliance obligations or voluntary commitments. They range from industrial conglomerates managing CCTS positions across multiple plants to technology companies purchasing voluntary offsets for their net-zero programmes.

Financial Intermediaries — banks, funds, and asset managers — have entered carbon markets as investment vehicles, providing liquidity, price discovery, and structured products. Their participation has increased market sophistication but also introduced speculative dynamics.

sections.heading: How Carbon Credit Prices Are Set
sections.content:
Carbon credit prices are not set by any single authority. They emerge from the interaction of supply and demand — but the factors shaping that supply and demand are more complex than in most commodity markets.

On the supply side, the cost of producing a carbon credit varies dramatically by project type. A large renewable energy project may generate credits at a cost of ₹250–400 per tonne. A direct air capture facility — which mechanically extracts CO₂ from the atmosphere — may cost ₹25,000 per tonne or more. The total supply of credits in any given period depends on how many projects have been verified and how many credits their registries have issued.

On the demand side, prices are shaped by the stringency of compliance obligations, the ambition of corporate net-zero targets, regulatory clarity, and general economic conditions. When economic activity slows, industrial emissions fall, and demand for compliance credits decreases — prices drop. When a government tightens its cap or raises its penalty rate, compliance buyers face more urgency — prices rise.

Quality commands a premium in the voluntary market. A credit from a rigorous, high-permanence, co-benefit-rich project will trade at a significant premium to a standardised credit with no additional attributes. ICVCM CCP-labelled credits — which meet the Integrity Council's Core Carbon Principles — trade at a premium to non-labelled credits because buyers trust they represent genuine climate impact.

Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating a new price tier. Credits that have received a Corresponding Adjustment (CA) from the host country government — meaning the host country formally agrees that the reduction counts only toward the buyer, not toward India's own national climate target — trade at a higher price than non-CA credits. As the Article 6 rulebook matures, CA-authorised credits are expected to command a growing premium.

For India's CCTS specifically, the government has established a price band: a floor of ₹600 per CCC and a ceiling of ₹1,200 per CCC. This band provides predictability for both buyers and sellers and prevents extreme price volatility in the market's early years.

infoBox.title: India CCTS Price Band — ₹600 to ₹1,200
infoBox.content: The BEE has established that Carbon Credit Certificates under India's CCTS trade within a regulated band of ₹600 (floor) to ₹1,200 (ceiling) per certificate on IEX and PXIL. This prevents the extreme price volatility seen in early EU ETS years and gives industrial facilities a predictable range for compliance budgeting.

sections.heading: The Global Carbon Market at a Glance
sections.content:
Carbon markets are now operating on every inhabited continent. The EU ETS remains the world's largest and most mature, covering over 10,000 industrial installations across 30 countries, with a market value exceeding €700 billion annually at recent price levels. Its price trajectory — from under €5 in early years to over €100 in 2023 — is the clearest evidence of what happens when a compliance cap is tightened consistently over time.

Beyond Europe, significant compliance markets operate in California (the California Cap-and-Trade Program, linked with Quebec), China (which launched the world's largest compliance market by covered emissions in 2021, though initially with low price levels and limited trading activity), South Korea, New Zealand, and several Canadian provinces.

The global voluntary carbon market was valued at approximately $2 billion in 2023. Growth projections vary widely, but the emergence of mandatory corporate disclosure requirements — the SEC's climate disclosure rule in the US, ISSB standards globally, and SEBI's BRSR Core in India — is expected to significantly increase voluntary demand as more companies face pressure to substantiate their net-zero claims with high-quality offsets.

India is a late but significant entrant. The CCTS covers some of India's most emissions-intensive industrial sectors. As the scheme matures and GEI targets tighten through the late 2020s, India's domestic carbon market is projected to become one of the largest in Asia. The infrastructure being built now — exchanges, registries, verification frameworks — will determine whether that market is transparent, liquid, and credible.

sections.heading: How EtherTrack Fits In
sections.content:
The gap EtherTrack addresses is not the absence of carbon credits or carbon markets in India. Both exist. The gap is the absence of accessible, integrated, transparent infrastructure for Indian businesses to participate in them.

Today, an Indian manufacturing company with CCTS compliance obligations navigates a fragmented landscape: emissions tracked in spreadsheets, CCC positions managed through broker calls, exchange orders placed manually on IEX or PXIL, compliance reports assembled by consultants, and retirement certificates arriving as PDFs with no independent verification pathway.

EtherTrack consolidates this into one platform. Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions are logged directly — via manual entry, CSV, ERP sync, or AI parser — and automatically feed the GHG inventory and carbon credit gap calculation. The exchange module provides a live order book and hybrid AMM liquidity pool for buying and selling credits, with payment in Indian Rupees via UPI, card, or bank transfer. The compliance module tracks GEI positions plant by plant, runs intra-group netting calculations to identify the most cost-efficient trading position before routing orders to IEX or PXIL. Every retirement generates an ISO 14064-3 certificate with a QR code resolving to a permanent on-chain record — verifiable by any auditor, independently.

For companies participating in the voluntary market, the same platform handles voluntary credit purchases, retirement, and the generation of BRSR Core, CDP, TCFD, and GHG Protocol reports from the same underlying dataset.

This is the infrastructure India's carbon market needs: transparent, accessible, and built for the compliance requirements that are already active — not the ones being discussed for 2030.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Carbon markets are trading systems where carbon credits are bought and sold. They exist to create a financial price for emissions — making it profitable to reduce them and costly not to.

There are two fundamentally different types: compliance markets (mandatory, government-created) and voluntary markets (optional, standards-based). They operate in parallel but serve different buyers and trade different instruments.

Compliance markets work through a cap — a total limit on emissions — with covered facilities required to hold enough credits to match their actual emissions or face penalties. India's CCTS uses an intensity-based variant, setting targets per unit of output rather than per facility.

Voluntary markets are driven by corporate net-zero commitments, investor pressure, and supply chain requirements. Credit quality varies enormously — due diligence on project type, methodology, verification, and registry is essential.

Carbon market participants include project developers, independent auditors (VVBs), registries, brokers, exchanges, corporate buyers, and financial intermediaries. Each plays a distinct role in the price discovery and settlement process.

Carbon credit prices are set by supply and demand, shaped by regulatory stringency, corporate commitment ambition, project economics, and credit quality. India's CCTS has a regulated price band of ₹600 to ₹1,200 per CCC.

India now has both a compliance market (CCTS, covering 9 industrial sectors) and active voluntary market participation. The infrastructure — registries, exchanges, verification frameworks — being established now will determine how credible and liquid India's carbon market becomes.
The next article in this series covers India's CCTS in detail — who is covered, how GEI targets work, what the compliance cycle looks like, and what non-compliance costs.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a compliance and voluntary carbon market?
faqs.answer: A compliance market is created by government legislation and participation is mandatory for covered industries. Companies that emit more than their allowed limit must buy credits or pay penalties. A voluntary market is created by independent standards bodies and participation is optional — companies choose to buy credits to meet net-zero commitments, satisfy investor expectations, or prepare for anticipated regulation.

faqs.question: Can voluntary carbon credits be used for CCTS compliance in India?
faqs.answer: No. India's CCTS compliance requires Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) issued specifically under the CCTS framework through GRID-India and traded on regulated exchanges like IEX and PXIL. Voluntary credits from international registries like Verra or Gold Standard cannot be submitted for CCTS compliance. They serve different markets with different rules.

faqs.question: What is the EU ETS and why does it matter for Indian businesses?
faqs.answer: The EU Emissions Trading System is the world's largest and most mature compliance carbon market, covering 10,000+ installations across 30 European countries. It matters for Indian businesses because of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will require Indian exporters in covered sectors — steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers — to pay a carbon price on exports to the EU equivalent to what European producers pay under the EU ETS. This makes understanding and managing carbon costs a trade competitiveness issue, not just a domestic compliance matter.

faqs.question: What is the ICVCM and why do CCP-labelled credits matter?
faqs.answer: The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) is an independent governance body that published the Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) — ten quality criteria that carbon credit programmes must meet to receive a CCP label. CCP-labelled credits trade at a premium because buyers trust they meet minimum standards of additionality, permanence, and verification rigour. Institutional buyers increasingly use CCP eligibility as a minimum screening criterion.

faqs.question: What is Article 6 of the Paris Agreement?
faqs.answer: Article 6 establishes the international framework for carbon credit trading under the Paris Agreement. Article 6.2 allows countries to trade carbon credits bilaterally. Article 6.4 establishes a UN-supervised crediting mechanism. The key concept is the Corresponding Adjustment (CA) — when a host country authorises a credit for international transfer, it agrees the reduction will not count toward its own national climate target. CA-authorised credits trade at a premium because they guarantee the reduction is counted only once globally.

faqs.question: How are carbon credit prices determined in India's CCTS?
faqs.answer: Under India's CCTS, Carbon Credit Certificates trade on IEX and PXIL within a regulated price band: a floor of ₹600 and a ceiling of ₹1,200 per CCC. Within this band, price is determined by market supply and demand — the volume of CCCs generated by outperforming facilities relative to the demand from underperforming facilities that need to buy to meet compliance. BEE can revise the price band at the start of each compliance cycle.
